ai.base_rate_used: Scenario page base rate: 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on EU sovereigns with a stable outlook going in (0%, and 0% as a lower bound on the wider count). S&P usually moves the outlook to negative before it cuts, so I start near zero and allow a small tail for an off-pattern cut.

factors.text: The reference class is clean on this point. S&P has not cut any of these six EU sovereigns straight from a stable outlook since 2014. The normal path is an outlook change first, and an outlook change alone resolves NO. This is the main reason I sit well below the market.

The fiscal and political backdrop is getting worse, which gives S&P cover to act. HCFP calls the 1.0% growth forecast optimistic and sees debt rising toward about 122%. Budget adoption by 31 December is close to a coin flip (50.5% and 49%). Marine Le Pen is priced at 41.1% to win in 2027. The OAT-Bund spread widened from 81.5bp to 96.7bp on the monthly series. This mostly argues for a negative outlook, but it keeps a direct cut possible.

Where the crowd may share an error: the 26.5% Polymarket price trades on thin volume (7345). The 31% Kalshi contract covers any agency through year-end, so it is wider than this question. Both seem to treat a bad fiscal story as if it meant an S&P cut on 27 Nov, and skip the outlook-first habit. The spread series is a degraded monthly average, and no gauge here is tested as a lead on rating actions.

ai.what_would_change_view: Any of these before 27 Nov would push me up toward the market: the government falls on a censure motion, PLF 2027 is rejected at first reading so a special law becomes the base case, or the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate. A confirmation that S&P's current outlook is already negative, not stable, would also break the reference class. A quiet first reading with the revenue part passed would push me toward affirm_stable.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The 'stable outlook going in' premise could be wrong, or S&P could decide that political paralysis before the 2027 election justifies an off-pattern cut. In either case the 0% reference class does not apply and the market's roughly one-in-four is closer to right.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page gives 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%) across 2006-2026. I give more weight to the subset since France lost its majority in 2022. The page shows that subset separately but does not quote it. Its branch notes say the 2024 and 2025 cycles both ended with a special law. The most relevant starting point is therefore roughly a coin flip for a minority government, well below 90.5%.

factors.text: Structural: a minority government since the 2024 dissolution. The last two budget cycles both missed 31 December and ended with a special law, the 2024 and 2025 pattern noted on the scenario page. The full-sample base rate of 90.5% mostly comes from years with a majority.

This budget is politically harder than usual. It has about 54 billion euros of consolidation, including a freeze of basic pensions and of the civil-service pay index. It lands just before the spring 2027 presidential race, in which Le Pen has launched her campaign and is priced at 41.1%. Opposition parties gain little from letting it pass, and a 49.3 invites a censure vote.

The government has tools to force it through. Kalshi prices use of Article 49.3 on the budget in 2026 at 66%. The Article 47 deadline of 10 December also opens a never-used ordinance route. This keeps the chance of adoption well above zero, provided the government survives.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if PS or LR publicly commit not to censure a 49.3 text, or if a joint committee agreement is reached in mid-December. I would move down if a censure motion gathers PS votes, if the revenue part fails at first reading in November, or if the government signals a special law as in 2024 and 2025.
ai.most_likely_wrong: Prediction markets at 50.5% and 49% may be right. The government may have secured a quiet non-censure deal, like the one that eventually passed the 2026 budget, and simply land it before Christmas this time, given the reputational cost of a third consecutive special law. My pre-election pessimism could then be overdone. The market signals themselves carry little tested evidence, and the official-optimism gauge is untested.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed probability for an RN win. Its reference class says the final-poll leader won 4 of 4 presidential run-offs, with an RMS poll error of 5.78 pp. That only helps once final polls exist, and the snapshot holds no polls six months out. As a last resort I start from market prices: on Polymarket, Le Pen at 41.1% plus Bardella at 1.7%; on Kalshi, Le Pen at 45% plus Bardella at 1.4%. Together that puts the RN candidate in the low-to-mid 40s.

factors.text: Markets price the RN candidate highest among single candidates. Le Pen has formally launched her campaign, and headlines are framing the race as hers to lose. That keeps the starting point near the market level. Note that the market splits RN odds between Le Pen and Bardella as though her ineligibility case were mostly settled; the question counts either name, so that split does not change the YES side.

The centre-right side is split across Lisnard at 19.6%, Philippe at 14.5%, Lagarde at 4.2% and others, and together they are close to the RN total. A run-off is usually a two-way race in which non-RN voters consolidate, and the signposts say that consolidation (withdrawals, sponsorship totals in March 2027) has not happened yet. I shade slightly below the market because fragmented anti-RN odds tend to understate the eventual run-off opponent.

The crowd's main gauge carries little evidential weight. The poll-versus-prediction-market gap is badged tested_no_lead, and prediction-market series in general are tested_no_lead. These markets have high volume but are untested as forecasters this far out. Fiscal strain could still feed the anti-incumbent vote: HCFP expects debt to rise toward about 122% of GDP and sees the 2029 deficit target as very unlikely to be met.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if second-round polls against the leading centre-right candidate show RN ahead by more than the 5.78 pp historical poll error, or if the centre-right stays split into March 2027. I would move down if one centre-right candidate consolidates (the others withdraw) and run-off polls show RN behind. A ruling that keeps Le Pen off the ballot would matter only if Bardella polled weaker than her.
ai.most_likely_wrong: I may be underrating RN. The old pattern of anti-RN voters uniting in the run-off may have weakened enough, under fiscal austerity and a polarised climate, that the market's low-to-mid 40s is too low rather than too high.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate; em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. My starting point is a judgement-based reference class: Brazil's recent self-set target cuts. The page lists two, in July 2015 and April 2024. Both came mid-year or with the April budget-guidelines bill, not in the first quarter of a year. On that basis a formal change inside a window ending 31 March is less likely than not, and I start around two-thirds YES before the evidence below.

factors.text: The government's own 2027 budget bill claims the target is met. It shows a surplus of R$83.4 billion (0.6% of GDP) counted for the target, against the R$73.2 billion target. A government that says it complies has little reason to send a bill cutting the target before the first bimonthly report around 22 March. The window also closes only about three months into the new term, and the 2015 and 2024 precedents came in July and April.

Independent numbers sit far below the target. The Focus 2027 primary-balance median is -0.4% of GDP, below even the lower tolerance bound; the most optimistic respondent is at 0.5. IFI sees a potential 2027 deficit of 1.0% of GDP and about R$40 billion of unbudgeted commitments. In IFI's scenario about R$35.7 billion of discretionary spending would have to be frozen. That gap makes a target cut, or a rule change via the still-pending budget-guidelines bill in December, a live option. It could arrive before March.

Bond markets repriced hard after Lula's run-off win. The 10y rose 255bp on day 1. In the week to 30 Oct the DI Jan-29 proxy rose 212bp and the longest fixed-rate Tesouro bond rose 233bp, to 15.29%. Investors are clearly pricing looser fiscal policy. These are price signals rather than tested forecasts: the Tesouro series is badged untested and the DI proxy is degraded. I give them some weight, not much.

ai.what_would_change_view: Toward NO: a PLN changing the 2027 target attached to the December budget-guidelines or budget (PLOA) vote; ministers publicly questioning the 0.5% target; a January finance minister who talks of rewriting LC 200/2023. Toward YES: the PLOA voted around 17 Dec without new exclusions, and a new finance minister who commits to the framework. The 20 Nov bimonthly report (RARDP) and its freeze size are an early read on intent.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The 2027 target may not yet be locked in, because the budget-guidelines bill is still pending. Congress or the government could lower the target there in December, quietly and before the new term even starts. That would turn my modal 'kept on paper' branch into NO well before the March report. The crowd's shared error may run the other way: markets price an immediate loosening of the actual fiscal path, but this question resolves on formal paperwork. A government can miss the target on Focus and IFI numbers for months without sending a bill to change it.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page's computed base rate (final-poll leader won 3 of 3 Mexican midterms; RMS poll error 4.12 pp) tells us who leads, not whether the coalition clears 334 of 500 seats. It does not answer this question directly. So I start from the same page's qualitative note: at the most recent midterm in the class, 2021, the governing coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. That is a starting point below even odds for a supermajority, with a simple majority as the default outcome.

factors.text: Midterm erosion is the default pattern. In 2021, the last midterm in em-macro's reference class, the governing coalition held a majority but lost two-thirds. Two-thirds needs both a high vote share (the page's signpost is above 55%) and favourable over-representation rulings from the INE, so several things must go right at once.

Polls have underestimated this coalition's strength before. In 2024 Sheinbaum led by 17pp and won by 33pp, and the congressional supermajority surprised markets badly. The primer names supermajorities that a two-candidate poll margin cannot capture as a known place where consensus errs. That keeps the YES tail fatter than a simple midterm-erosion story implies.

The crowd sees Morena as dominant: 87.5% on Polymarket and 86% on Kalshi that it wins the most seats, with PAN at 7.8%. That argues against the coalition losing its majority. But these are related-only contracts that say nothing about the 334-seat line, and prediction-market series carry a tested_no_lead badge, so I give them little weight beyond the low lose_majority branch.

ai.what_would_change_view: Mid-2027 polls putting the coalition's combined vote above 55% would push me toward or above even odds. Below 45% would raise lose_majority. An INE ruling that tightens or loosens the coalition over-representation rules (the 2024 dispute) would move the seat maths directly. Candidate registration and precampaigns in January 2027 will be the first hard read on alliance arrangements in key districts.
ai.most_likely_wrong: I may be anchoring too much on midterm erosion. If the coalition repeats its 2024 pattern of beating polls, and the seat allocation again rewards the alliance, two-thirds could be the more likely outcome. The market's dominance pricing would then be the better guide, and I would be underweighting a known polling blind spot that I flagged myself.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: this is the agreement's first review cycle, and em-macro has no trade-agreement events. As a last resort I start from market prices on the 2026 review. Those markets put a 16-year extension in 2026 at 8% (pm:2761052) and 12% (ks:KXUSMCAOUTCOMES-27-16Y), against 13% for a US withdrawal notice. They resolve on a different, earlier window, and the 2026 review has already passed without an extension.

factors.text: The first chance to extend has already been missed. The 2026 review ended without a 16-year extension, which is why annual joint reviews now apply. A US administration that passed on extending once has shown it prefers the leverage of a recurring review over locking in a long term.

USTR is actively using the agreement's enforcement tools against Mexico, such as the labour-rights case at Madobox. In the same week it signed a memorandum of understanding with Mexico, so engagement continues. This looks like managing the deal case by case, which fits continued annual reviews better than a clean written extension from all three countries.

Markets give a revised trilateral deal some chance: 24% for 2026 (ks:KXUSMCAOUTCOMES-27-TRI). A renegotiated text could be paired with an extension, which keeps YES from being remote. But these are thin, low-volume contracts, and prediction-market gauges are badged tested_no_lead, so I give them little weight.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if USTR's 2027 public consultation (placeholder date around 1 Feb 2027) or its report recommends extension, or if US tariffs on Mexican goods are cut below 10%; both are signposts on the scenario page. I would move down if the US proposes separate US-Mexico and US-Canada texts, or officials describe withdrawal as leverage. A firm date for the next bilateral round (the 30 Nov placeholder) would also help.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The US could decide it has extracted enough concessions, through a revised deal or side agreements, and grant the written extension at the 1 Jul 2027 review to claim a win. Under that reading the 2026 miss was a negotiating pause, not a preference for annual reviews. The crowd and I may both be anchoring too heavily on the 2026 outcome. There is also a shared blind spot in the other direction: the peso is calm at 18.7592 and leveraged funds are long the peso at the 79.5th percentile (a tested_no_lead gauge). That suggests little tail risk is priced, and an off-calendar US trade announcement could change the picture faster than the scheduled review.

degraded.effect: Same Banxico series IDs, read from the public chart endpoint that backs banxico.org.mx graphs. It is unofficial and undocumented, so it can change without notice, and it serves the latest values only as of the page cache (can lag the API by hours).
degraded.upgrade: add the BANXICO_TOKEN secret under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions; the next data run uses it and every feature switches over by itself

calculator.default_basis: today's level plus the expected move of the good and bad branches

notes: Moves marked assumption are judgements or rescalings, not em-macro estimates.
